AI decides what it wants to do. A deterministic risk/execution layer decides whether it is allowed to do it and how the transaction is executed.

That separation is probably the single biggest thing to get right.

Current Solana infrastructure makes this especially relevant: transactions have explicit prioritization economics, failed transactions still consume fees, and real-time account/block subscriptions are available for event-driven systems. Jupiter is also moving its swap stack forward, so the system should not hard-code itself around an obsolete integration such as Ultra; Jupiter currently says Ultra is superseded by Swap V2.

Here is the list I'd hand to a coding model.

Autonomous Solana Trading System — Deep Design Checklist
1. Define the actual product before building the bot

The product is not:

“Give me $1,000 and AI trades it.”

The real product is:

“Give the system a capital allocation and a risk mandate; the system continuously observes the market, generates opportunities, evaluates them, sizes positions, executes trades, manages positions, and shuts itself down when its assumptions become invalid.”

That distinction matters enormously.

The system should therefore have explicit concepts for:

capital
available capital
deployed capital
reserved capital
realized PnL
unrealized PnL
daily PnL
rolling PnL
drawdown
exposure
liquidity exposure
strategy exposure
token exposure
execution costs
slippage
failed transactions
gas/priority costs
confidence
market regime
strategy health
system health

Don't reduce everything to “balance.”

2. Three modes should share one core

Your three ideas are actually excellent because they let you compare fundamentally different approaches.

Mode A — Autonomous AI Trader

LLM/AI receives access to market-analysis tools and potentially Rust/Solana tools.

Its job:

investigate
reason
identify opportunities
compare opportunities
formulate a thesis
decide whether to trade
determine desired position
manage positions
adapt its behavior

But do not let the AI directly own the final authority to move money.

The AI should make something conceptually equivalent to:

“I want to enter TOKEN X with Y exposure because Z.”

Then another system determines:

“Is that legal within this strategy's risk limits?”

Then another system determines:

“What is the best executable transaction?”

This creates a chain like:

AI → trade proposal → risk engine → execution engine → transaction → verification

rather than:

AI → wallet → money gone

3. Mode B — Pure software strategy engine

This should be your control experiment.

No LLM.

Signals might include:

momentum
volume
liquidity changes
holder concentration
wallet flows
buy/sell imbalance
price acceleration
volatility
liquidity migration
new pool creation
whale movements
launch activity
market-wide conditions
correlated-token movement
order-flow proxies
transaction activity
arbitrage relationships
funding/basis if derivatives are involved
time-of-day effects
regime changes

This mode is extremely important because it answers:

Does the trading system actually possess an edge, or is the AI merely narrating randomness?

You need this benchmark.

4. Mode C — Specialized professional-trader AI

This is potentially the most interesting mode.

But I would not initially conceptualize it as:

“Fine-tune GPT into Warren Buffett + Citadel + Solana whale.”

Instead think:

General LLM + structured market state + trading memory + specialized knowledge + evaluation + constraints + feedback

The model should effectively learn:

what information matters
what information doesn't
how different market regimes behave
which signals have historically mattered
which signals are deceptive
when not to trade
how much uncertainty is acceptable
how to update beliefs
how to learn from previous trades

The critical concept is that the model needs persistent state, not simply a better prompt.

Modern agent frameworks explicitly support tools, persistent sessions, guardrails, structured outputs, tracing/evaluation, and human approval workflows, which maps surprisingly well onto this architecture.

5. Separate “research AI” from “trading AI”

This is a huge consideration.

You may ultimately want several agents.

Market researcher

Finds:

new tokens
new narratives
ecosystem developments
smart-money movements
unusual activity
liquidity events
protocol developments
social/news information
Quant analyst

Analyzes:

price
volume
volatility
liquidity
correlations
historical patterns
On-chain analyst

Analyzes:

wallets
token holders
program interactions
liquidity pools
transfers
smart-money behavior
Risk manager

Asks:

“Regardless of how attractive this trade looks, is it permitted?”

Execution specialist

Asks:

“Given that we're allowed to make the trade, what's the optimal execution?”

Portfolio manager

Looks at:

“What should the entire portfolio look like?”

Meta-agent

Potentially decides:

“Which strategy should currently have capital?”

That becomes much more interesting than one gigantic AI.

6. Never give the AI unlimited tool access

This is one of the biggest things I would change from your original idea.

You said:

“AI that has access to all of the Rust tools to make the best traders.”

I'd strongly distinguish:

Read tools

Safe-ish:

inspect account
inspect program
inspect token
inspect transactions
inspect pool
inspect wallet
query historical data
simulate transaction
calculate metrics
fetch market state
Analysis tools
calculate volatility
calculate liquidity
compare assets
backtest hypothesis
identify anomalies
score wallets
calculate expected value
Proposal tools
propose trade
propose allocation
propose exit
propose hedge
Execution tools

Extremely restricted:

swap
sell
buy
transfer
revoke
interact with protocol
Administrative tools

Even more restricted:

change strategy
change risk limits
change wallet permissions
modify capital allocation
update code
modify infrastructure

The AI should not have symmetrical authority across these layers.

Modern agent systems themselves recognize the distinction between tools and tool guardrails/approval boundaries.

7. AI-generated transaction ≠ executable transaction

A model might say:

buy 4 SOL of X

That isn't enough.

The execution pipeline needs to independently determine:

exact asset
exact amount
route
expected output
minimum output
slippage
price impact
liquidity
priority fee
transaction freshness
account state
token program
pool state
transaction simulation result
maximum permitted loss
whether market conditions changed since analysis

The final transaction should be generated by deterministic infrastructure.

The AI is proposing intent.

The execution layer translates intent into reality.

8. Build an immutable risk layer

This should be the dictator above every strategy.

Risk limits could include:

Portfolio limits
max capital deployed
max portfolio drawdown
max daily loss
max weekly loss
max open positions
max correlated exposure
max single-token exposure
Trade limits
maximum trade size
minimum liquidity
maximum price impact
maximum slippage
minimum expected edge
minimum confidence
maximum transaction cost
Token limits
minimum liquidity
maximum holder concentration
maximum creator allocation
maximum insider concentration
suspicious mint authority
freeze authority
transfer restrictions
Token-2022 extensions
blacklist/whitelist behavior
unusual program ownership

Solana's Token Extensions / Token-2022 ecosystem makes this particularly important because token behavior can include additional functionality beyond what a simple SPL-token mental model assumes.

9. Risk level should NOT simply mean position size

This is a really important product decision.

“Low risk” shouldn't merely mean:

trade 10% of capital.

It should alter the entire behavior of the system.

For example:

Conservative
fewer opportunities
higher confidence requirement
deeper liquidity requirement
smaller positions
lower turnover
lower slippage tolerance
stricter drawdown
more capital in reserve
Balanced
moderate opportunity set
moderate exposure
moderate drawdown tolerance
Aggressive
broader opportunity set
higher position concentration
higher acceptable volatility
faster strategy adaptation
larger exposure

But even “aggressive” should have hard catastrophic boundaries.

10. Add a “do nothing” decision

This sounds trivial.

It isn't.

The bot should explicitly have:

NO TRADE

as one of its outputs.

Otherwise an AI can develop implicit pressure to always produce activity.

You want:

BUY / SELL / HOLD / WAIT / REDUCE / EXIT / DO NOTHING

not simply:

BUY / SELL

11. The AI needs to understand uncertainty

Don't allow:

“This will probably pump.”

You want something closer to:

thesis
evidence
counter-evidence
expected upside
expected downside
probability distribution
confidence
invalidation condition
time horizon
liquidity assumptions
execution assumptions

Most importantly:

What would prove the thesis wrong?

That question should be first-class.

12. Build a market-regime engine

This could become one of the most valuable components.

Markets behave differently during:

extreme bull markets
slow bull markets
sideways markets
panic selloffs
meme rotations
liquidity droughts
high-volatility periods
BTC-driven markets
Solana-specific rotations
major narrative rotations
post-launch mania
post-collapse environments

The same strategy can have radically different expectancy across regimes.

The system should therefore ask:

What kind of market are we currently in?

before asking:

What should I buy?

13. Strategy selection may matter more than trade selection

Instead of:

“Which token should I buy?”

the higher-level question can be:

“Which strategy has the highest expected risk-adjusted return right now?”

For example:

momentum strategy
mean-reversion strategy
breakout strategy
liquidity event strategy
wallet-following strategy
arbitrage strategy
trend strategy
event strategy
market-neutral strategy

Then:

Market regime → strategy selection → opportunity selection → position sizing → execution

That is much more sophisticated.

14. The system should be capable of retiring strategies

This is absolutely critical.

A strategy shouldn't live forever because it once made money.

Track:

rolling Sharpe
rolling Sortino
hit rate
expectancy
drawdown
slippage-adjusted return
transaction-cost-adjusted return
regime-specific performance
performance degradation

Then allow states such as:

ACTIVE → DEGRADED → PAUSED → RETIRED

15. Don't let the AI “learn” directly from PnL blindly

This can create catastrophic feedback loops.

Example:

Bot loses $5,000.

AI concludes:

“I need to trade more aggressively.”

Loss increases.

AI becomes even more aggressive.

Eventually catastrophic failure.

Learning should therefore occur through controlled evaluation, not emotional reinforcement.

16. Build a trading memory

Every decision should become structured historical data.

For every trade store:

market state before trade
market state after trade
strategy
AI reasoning summary
signals
confidence
position size
entry
exit
fees
slippage
expected outcome
actual outcome
MFE
MAE
duration
exit reason
thesis invalidation
market regime

Then the system can eventually ask:

“What happened historically when these conditions occurred?”

That's far more useful than simply dumping thousands of previous conversations into context.

17. Distinguish prediction from explanation

This is a major AI issue.

An LLM can produce an incredibly convincing explanation for a trade that happened to be profitable.

That doesn't prove the explanation caused the prediction.

You therefore need separate measurements for:

Prediction

Did the system correctly anticipate the market?

Decision

Did it choose the correct action?

Execution

Did it execute that decision well?

Explanation

Can it articulate why?

Those are four different capabilities.

18. Build an offline research environment

Before live capital, the system should be able to replay historical markets.

Give the system:

historical state at time T

and forbid it from seeing:

information after T

Then ask:

What would you have done?

This is essential for avoiding look-ahead bias.

Test:

different market periods
different liquidity conditions
bull
bear
sideways
crashes
mania
new-token launches
congestion
failed transactions
extreme slippage
19. Backtesting must simulate reality

A naive backtest:

Buy at price X → sell at price Y

is almost worthless for fast Solana trading.

You need to account for:

slippage
liquidity
price impact
fees
priority fees
failed transactions
stale quotes
transaction latency
partial execution
route changes
disappearing liquidity
spreads
adverse selection

Solana's priority-fee mechanics are especially relevant because prioritization fees are based on requested compute limits/price, and fees can still be charged on failed transactions.

20. Build a shadow mode

Before allowing real capital:

AI makes decisions but cannot trade.

Record:

“At 14:32:10 the AI would have bought X.”

Then measure what would have happened.

Do this for substantial time.

Then:

AI makes real decisions with tiny capital.

Then gradually increase exposure.

21. Build multiple simulation modes

You should eventually have:

Historical replay

Past markets.

Paper trading

Live market, fake capital.

Shadow trading

System makes real-time decisions but doesn't execute.

Tiny-capital mode

Real execution with minimal capital.

Production mode

Normal allocation.

Emergency mode

No new trades, only risk reduction.

22. Transaction safety deserves its own subsystem

Solana is extremely fast, which is an advantage and a hazard.

The bot needs to understand:

commitment level
blockhash lifetime
transaction expiration
retries
duplicate execution
confirmation
account changes
simulation
stale state
RPC disagreement

Real-time subscriptions can be used to react to account changes and block activity, but the system should still have reconciliation rather than assuming every event stream is perfect.

23. Build redundant data sources

Never make one RPC/provider your single source of truth.

Consider independent sources for:

RPC
market prices
token metadata
liquidity
transaction data
wallet intelligence
social/news information

You want to detect:

“Provider A says X happened, but Provider B says otherwise.”

That discrepancy itself can become a health signal.

24. The execution engine should know about liquidity

Your strategy could be right and still lose money.

Example:

AI predicts:

+20%

But entering moves price +8%.

Exiting moves price -10%.

Actual trade:

negative.

Therefore expected return must be:

gross alpha − fees − slippage − price impact − execution risk

not simply predicted price movement.

25. Think carefully about MEV

This is especially important in Solana trading.

Your execution layer should eventually understand:

transaction ordering
sandwich-like risks
arbitrage competition
private submission
bundles
leader/validator behavior
priority fees
execution timing

Do not assume:

“I generated the transaction, therefore I got the price.”

26. Build an execution-quality score

Every transaction can receive a score based on:

expected price
actual price
slippage
latency
fee
priority fee
failure/retry
price movement during execution

Then you can answer:

“Is our alpha bad, or is our execution bad?”

That distinction is invaluable.

27. Wallet architecture

For a private prototype, decide extremely early:

Who controls the private key?
Where is it stored?
Can the AI ever access it?
Can software retrieve it?
Can execution be limited?
Can withdrawals occur?
Can someone modify the trading permissions?

For an autonomous system, I would conceptually separate:

decision authority

from

fund movement authority

and make emergency withdrawal/control mechanisms independent of the AI.

28. Build a kill switch that does not depend on the AI

This should be physically/logically above the trading stack.

Conditions might include:

abnormal loss
abnormal transaction failure
corrupted market data
RPC instability
unexpected program interaction
wallet compromise indicators
liquidity collapse
strategy drift
model malfunction
infrastructure malfunction

The AI should not be able to override the kill switch.

29. Model failures are not the only failures

You need to assume:

The AI will sometimes be wrong.

But also:

The AI can be perfectly correct while the system fails.

Examples:

stale data
transaction not landing
wrong token address
incorrect decimals
RPC outage
manipulated metadata
unexpected token behavior
liquidity disappears
execution route changes
duplicated order
incorrect state synchronization

This is why the risk/execution layer needs to be deterministic.

30. Treat token security as a trading signal

Particularly for Solana/memecoin trading, analyze:

mint authority
freeze authority
token program
Token-2022 extensions
holder concentration
creator holdings
creator wallet history
liquidity ownership
liquidity lock/burn state
suspicious transfers
wallet clusters
unusual authority changes
transfer restrictions
blacklist behavior
metadata manipulation

Token-2022's extension model specifically means your token-analysis layer should inspect the extensions present rather than assuming every token behaves identically.

31. Wallet intelligence could become its own product

Potentially maintain classifications such as:

smart money
insider
market maker
bot
sniper
deployer
influencer
retail
probable sybil
toxic wallet

Then study:

Which wallet behaviors actually predict future returns?

Don't assume “whale bought = bullish.”

The model needs to learn which wallet classes matter.

32. Don't accidentally create a fake “smart money” system

A wallet that made 10 successful trades may simply have been lucky.

You need:

longitudinal performance
sample size
market-regime adjustment
risk adjustment
survivorship correction
latency correction

Otherwise your wallet intelligence becomes glorified hindsight.

33. Separate alpha data from execution data

Alpha data asks:

What is likely to happen?

Execution data asks:

Can we profitably trade it?

These should be evaluated separately.

34. Build a proper portfolio manager

Eventually the system shouldn't think about trades independently.

Imagine:

Position A has expected return +15%.

Position B has expected return +12%.

But both are effectively the same exposure.

Taking both may be worse than taking one.

Portfolio decisions should consider:

correlation
concentration
liquidity
volatility
covariance
expected return
downside
capital efficiency
35. Consider an ensemble architecture

One model saying:

BUY

is fragile.

Potentially have:

Technical model → BUY

On-chain model → BUY

Market-regime model → BULLISH

Risk model → ALLOWED

Execution model → EXECUTABLE

Then:

Portfolio engine → allocate

This is much more robust.

36. AI disagreement can become a feature

Instead of suppressing disagreement, measure it.

For example:

Technical AI:

82% bullish

On-chain AI:

35% bullish

Risk AI:

high risk

Execution AI:

poor liquidity

That might correctly produce:

NO TRADE

rather than forcing consensus.

37. The AI should have a confidence budget

Confidence should have consequences.

For example:

High confidence:

→ larger allocation within hard limits

Low confidence:

→ smaller allocation

Very uncertain:

→ observe only

Importantly:

confidence should be empirically calibrated.

If the AI says 80% confidence 100 times, approximately 80 of those predictions should actually succeed under the defined event.

Otherwise “confidence” is meaningless.

38. Consider time horizons

Your trader may need distinct horizons:

milliseconds/seconds
minutes
hours
days

An LLM is probably not the component you want making millisecond-level execution decisions.

AI is much more interesting for:

contextual analysis
regime identification
strategic selection
hypothesis generation
higher-level portfolio decisions

while deterministic systems handle ultra-low-latency execution.

39. Consider latency as an explicit variable

Measure:

information arrival → model decision → transaction construction → signing → broadcast → inclusion → confirmation

Then track where time is being lost.

You may discover your “AI strategy” is profitable conceptually but impossible because your pipeline is 800ms slower than competitors.

40. AI tool latency needs to be measured

LLM calls aren't free.

Track:

inference latency
tool latency
data retrieval latency
total decision time
token usage
API cost
failure rate

Then calculate:

Does the expected alpha exceed the cost of obtaining the decision?

41. Use cheap models for cheap decisions

Not every observation deserves the biggest model.

Potential architecture:

fast model → screening

↓ only interesting opportunities

stronger model → analysis

↓ only high-value opportunities

portfolio/risk system → approval

This dramatically changes economics.

42. Specialized model doesn't necessarily mean fine-tuning

There are several ways to create your “professional trader” system:

Prompt specialization

Instructions + structured methodology.

Retrieval

Give the model specialized trading knowledge.

Persistent memory

Give it historical experience.

Tool specialization

Give it market/on-chain tools.

Distillation

Train a smaller model on decisions generated by stronger systems.

Fine-tuning

Teach specific behaviors from high-quality examples.

Ensemble

Combine different specialized models.

You shouldn't assume fine-tuning is automatically the best approach.

43. Create a “trader constitution”

This could become one of the most useful artifacts in the project.

Define the AI's permanent principles:

never revenge trade
don't trade solely because of FOMO
don't increase risk after losses
don't assume liquidity remains constant
challenge your own thesis
prefer no trade to low-edge trade
explicitly quantify uncertainty
separate evidence from speculation
respect risk limits
stop when assumptions become invalid

Then evaluate every model against the constitution.

44. Build adversarial evaluation

Don't only ask:

“Can it make money?”

Ask:

“Can I trick it into making stupid trades?”

Test:

fake signals
contradictory signals
manipulated token names
misleading metadata
malicious tool outputs
spoofed market information
sudden liquidity removal
impossible price data
conflicting RPC results
fake social narratives

AI tool systems have recognized the importance of guardrails around tool invocations specifically because tool access creates a new attack surface.

45. Assume the market will attack your assumptions

Once the bot becomes successful, other participants may adapt.

Your edge can disappear because:

bots copy behavior
liquidity moves
market makers adjust
launch mechanics change
alpha becomes crowded
competitors detect your patterns

Therefore track:

Is our edge decaying?

46. Beware of reflexivity

If your bot becomes large enough:

your own trades affect the market.

The strategy's historical behavior can therefore stop being valid at larger capital.

You need scalability tests:

$100

$1k

$10k

$100k

$1m

The strategy may have completely different returns at each scale.

47. Capital allocation itself can become intelligent

Instead of users choosing:

Mode A 100%

allow:

Mode A: 20%

Mode B: 50%

Mode C: 30%

and dynamically adjust allocations based on strategy performance.

Eventually:

Meta-strategy chooses which strategies deserve capital.

That is potentially much more powerful than one “super trader.”

48. Strategy competition / tournament

This is something I would seriously consider.

Run many strategies simultaneously using paper capital.

For example:

Strategy A
Strategy B
Strategy C
AI A
AI B
AI C

Give each a virtual account.

Measure:

return
drawdown
Sharpe
Sortino
stability
execution efficiency

Then promote/demote strategies automatically.

Essentially:

evolutionary selection of trading agents.

49. Don't optimize purely for ROI

This is one of the easiest traps.

A strategy returning +300% with a catastrophic 95% drawdown might be worse than:

+60% return

with:

15% drawdown.

You want a multi-objective fitness function involving:

return
volatility
drawdown
tail risk
liquidity
turnover
execution quality
consistency
50. Tail risk deserves special treatment

Crypto has fat tails.

You need to ask:

What happens if the market moves 30% against us in one minute?

And:

What happens if liquidity disappears entirely?

Normal stop-loss logic doesn't necessarily protect you from gaps/liquidity collapse.

51. Define catastrophic events explicitly

Examples:

liquidity falls below threshold
transaction failure rate spikes
wallet authority changes
unexpected token transfer behavior
market data divergence
RPC divergence
strategy drawdown threshold
model malfunction
anomalous transaction behavior

Then define:

what happens next?

Don't leave that to the AI.

52. Reconciliation system

The bot needs to continuously reconcile:

what we think happened

vs.

what actually happened on-chain

This should be independent of the strategy engine.

For example:

Internal ledger:

bought 2.3 SOL

Blockchain:

actually received 2.17 SOL worth

The reconciliation system catches that.

53. Immutable audit trail

For every decision you should eventually be able to answer:

What did the bot know?

What did it believe?

What did it decide?

Why did it decide it?

What risk rules were checked?

What transaction was generated?

What transaction actually landed?

What happened afterward?

This is enormously valuable both technically and legally.

54. Observability

Build dashboards for:

System
uptime
latency
RPC health
error rate
transaction success
Strategy
trades
win rate
expectancy
drawdown
Sharpe
turnover
AI
calls
latency
decisions
confidence
tool usage
rejected actions
hallucination/error rate
Execution
slippage
price impact
priority fees
route quality
failed transactions
Portfolio
exposure
liquidity
concentration
realized/unrealized PnL
55. Explainability should be built for debugging, not marketing

A dangerous assumption is:

“The AI needs to explain itself to users.”

What you really need first is:

“We need to understand what caused this decision.”

Those aren't identical.

Store structured decision factors.

Don't rely exclusively on a model-generated paragraph like:

“I felt bullish because…”

56. Don't let user-facing explanations become the source of truth

The trading engine should provide a factual decision record.

Then the LLM can generate a human-readable explanation from that record.

That prevents the AI from retrospectively inventing reasons.

57. Current Solana integration should be abstraction-based

Don't hard-code the architecture around one provider.

Create abstraction layers for:

RPC
transaction submission
quote engine
liquidity sources
token metadata
chain indexing
market data
wallet intelligence

That matters because the Solana developer stack is evolving quickly. Jupiter's current documentation, for example, explicitly marks Ultra as superseded by Swap V2.

58. Don't conflate “Solana tools” with “trading edge”

Having access to Rust/Solana tooling is not an edge.

Access to:

account state
programs
transactions
token data
simulations

gives the AI capability.

The edge comes from:

information + interpretation + timing + execution + risk management

The system needs to discover which combinations actually produce predictive power.

59. Research should continuously search for new signals

Long-term, one of the coolest possibilities is:

AI as quantitative researcher.

The AI doesn't just trade.

It asks:

“Which variables seem predictive?”

Then:

“Can I formulate a hypothesis?”

Then:

“Can the research environment test it?”

Then:

“Does it survive out-of-sample evaluation?”

Then:

“Can it become a strategy?”

This is potentially much more interesting than simply making an LLM trade.

60. But research AI must be sandboxed

The research agent should be able to:

analyze data
form hypotheses
run backtests
create strategy candidates
evaluate strategies

but not automatically deploy a strategy to real capital.

Deployment should require passing predefined gates.

61. Strategy promotion pipeline

Something like:

Idea

↓

Backtest

↓

Out-of-sample

↓

Walk-forward test

↓

Paper trading

↓

Shadow trading

↓

Tiny capital

↓

Limited production

↓

Full production

This could become one of the core systems of the entire product.

62. Prevent overfitting

This is perhaps the biggest quant danger.

An AI given enough historical data can discover unbelievable “strategies” that are simply statistical accidents.

Use:

train/test separation
walk-forward validation
untouched evaluation periods
multiple market regimes
parameter stability tests
sensitivity analysis
perturbation tests

The question isn't:

“Did it work historically?”

It's:

“Does the edge survive when we change the conditions?”

63. Track strategy provenance

Every strategy should know:

where it came from
which hypothesis generated it
which data trained/evaluated it
which version it is
which model created it
when it was deployed
what changed
what performance it produced

This becomes incredibly important once you have dozens or hundreds of strategies.

64. Model versioning

You should be able to say:

GPT Trader v17 made these 381 trades.

Then compare:

GPT Trader v18.

And:

What changed?

Never silently swap the brain while pretending performance is continuous.

65. AI model independence

Eventually test:

GPT-family model
another frontier model
smaller local model
quant model
traditional ML model

You might discover:

the best system isn't one model.

It may be:

LLM + gradient boosting + time-series model + deterministic signals

66. Don't assume an LLM should predict prices

A very interesting architecture is:

Traditional models predict numbers.
LLM interprets context.

For example:

Quant model:

expected return = +4.3%

On-chain model:

insider-risk = 0.81

Regime model:

momentum regime = strong

LLM:

“Given these inputs, should capital be allocated?”

That may be significantly more robust than asking GPT:

“What will SOL do?”

67. Consider LLMs as policy engines

Instead of:

“Predict price.”

ask:

“Given this state and these possible actions, which action maximizes expected risk-adjusted return subject to these constraints?”

That's a much cleaner formulation.

68. Market state should be structured

Give the AI a canonical market-state representation rather than thousands of random tool outputs.

Conceptually:

MarketState

macro condition
Solana condition
token state
liquidity state
wallet state
technical signals
portfolio state
execution state
risk state

Then the AI reasons over a coherent state.

69. Tool output quality matters enormously

A brilliant AI with bad tools becomes a terrible trader.

Tool outputs should be:

normalized
timestamped
source-labeled
confidence-scored
internally consistent
machine-readable

And the AI should know:

how fresh is this information?

70. Every piece of market data should have a timestamp

This sounds minor.

It isn't.

An AI might receive:

liquidity = $400k

but that number might actually be 15 seconds old.

In memecoin markets, 15 seconds can be an eternity.

So every observation should conceptually include:

value + timestamp + source + freshness

71. Build “information age” into decision making

The system should know:

price data = 200ms old

wallet data = 4 seconds old

social data = 3 minutes old

fundamental context = 2 hours old

Different signals have different decay rates.

72. Consider social data carefully

If you use:

X
Telegram
Discord
Reddit
news
influencers

you need to distinguish:

information

from

manipulation

and:

correlated reposting

from

independent confirmation

50 accounts repeating the same statement may be one information source.

73. Information provenance

Every important signal should ideally have:

source
time
reliability score
originality score
historical predictive value

Then the AI can learn:

“This source has historically been wrong 70% of the time.”

That is much more valuable than simply feeding it content.

74. Consider market manipulation detection as a separate problem

The trader should ask:

Is this move real?

rather than:

Is this move bullish?

Potential signals:

synchronized wallet behavior
fake volume
circular transfers
liquidity manipulation
concentrated ownership
suspicious timing
coordinated social activity
75. Security model for the AI itself

You have to assume an adversarial environment.

Potential attack surfaces:

malicious token metadata
prompt injection through external text
malicious tool output
compromised API
malicious RPC data
poisoned research data
manipulated social content

The AI should never blindly treat external text as instructions.

76. Make tool permissions contextual

For example:

Research mode:

read-only

Paper trading:

simulate only

Production:

limited trading

Administrative:

human approval

This maps nicely to the capabilities modern agent frameworks expose around tool permissions, guardrails, approvals, and structured tool calls.

77. Consider human override even if the final product is autonomous

You don't necessarily want humans making individual trades.

But humans should potentially be able to:

pause system
lower risk
shut down strategy
withdraw funds
inspect decisions
approve major configuration changes

Autonomous ≠ uncontrollable.

78. Public product architecture should be different from private prototype

Private:

one wallet → one system → your capital

Public:

users → accounts → policies → permissions → strategies → execution → reporting

That becomes substantially more complicated.

79. Custody is a giant architectural fork

Before public launch decide whether you are:

Non-custodial

Users maintain control of funds.

or

Custodial

Your infrastructure controls customer assets.

That difference affects:

security
compliance
liability
infrastructure
trust
operational procedures

You should make this decision with legal counsel, not after you've already built the product around one assumption.

Current U.S. regulatory treatment of crypto has also evolved materially in 2026, including a joint SEC/CFTC interpretation concerning crypto assets and transactions, so assumptions from older crypto regulatory guides may now be outdated.

80. Legal should be designed into the architecture

Not:

build everything → call lawyer

Consider early:

custody
investment advice
discretionary trading
performance fees
subscriptions
user funds
securities exposure
derivatives
geographic restrictions
KYC/AML
tax reporting
marketing claims
disclosures
auditability

FinCEN has long distinguished users from administrators/exchangers, while current SEC/CFTC activity continues to refine how different crypto activities are treated.

81. Be extremely careful with marketing

The product should not implicitly promise:

“AI makes money automatically.”

The honest framing is closer to:

“An autonomous system that manages a defined trading strategy under explicit risk constraints.”

This isn't just legal caution.

It also forces you to build the right product.

82. Don't hide drawdowns

Make drawdown a first-class metric.

Users should eventually be able to see:

return
max drawdown
recovery time
volatility
worst day
worst trade
exposure
number of trades

A system that hides these numbers will eventually lose trust.

83. Consider a verifiable track record

If this becomes public, the strongest marketing asset won't be:

“Our AI is incredible.”

It will be:

verifiable on-chain performance with a complete history.

Users should theoretically be able to inspect the actual wallet and transactions.

That creates a much stronger trust mechanism.

84. But don't confuse wallet performance with strategy performance

Suppose strategy earns +100%.

Maybe the market earned +180%.

Then the strategy actually underperformed.

Benchmark against:

SOL
BTC
relevant Solana index
buy-and-hold
alternative strategies
85. Opportunity cost matters

A bot should be evaluated against:

What else could the capital have done?

Not merely:

Did the bot make money?

86. Build a capital-efficiency metric

Measure:

return per unit of capital + risk + liquidity consumed

A strategy generating 10% using 95% of capital may be worse than one generating 8% with 20%.

87. Think about minimum viable capital

Different strategies have different capital requirements.

A strategy can work with:

$500

but fail at:

$500,000

because the market can't absorb it.

The system should know its capacity.

88. Capacity should be strategy-specific

Each strategy needs:

minimum capital
optimal capital
maximum capital
liquidity ceiling

Then the allocation engine shouldn't give it more capital simply because it's performing well.

89. Add “strategy crowding” detection

If several strategies are producing nearly identical trades, you're not actually diversified.

Measure:

trade overlap
portfolio correlation
signal correlation
drawdown correlation

Ten strategies can secretly be one strategy.

90. The coolest long-term architecture

If I were thinking about the project at the highest level, I'd picture:

DATA LAYER

↓

MARKET STATE ENGINE

↓

RESEARCH / SIGNAL ENGINES

↓

MULTIPLE TRADING AGENTS

↓

PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZER

↓

RISK ENGINE

↓

EXECUTION ENGINE

↓

SOLANA

↓

RECONCILIATION

↓

PERFORMANCE / LEARNING

↓

RESEARCH ENGINE

and then that loops forever.

That's the actual autonomous system.

91. Your three modes can sit inside this
Mode 1 — AI Agent

AI → signals → portfolio → risk → execution

Mode 2 — Deterministic Bot

signals → portfolio → risk → execution

Mode 3 — Specialized Trader

specialized AI → signals → portfolio → risk → execution

Everything underneath remains identical.

That is important because then you can experimentally answer:

Is AI actually improving trading performance?

92. Build A/B comparisons into the platform from day one

You should be able to compare:

AI trader

vs

quant trader

vs

specialized AI

under identical conditions.

Same:

capital
market
execution
fees
risk constraints

Then measure the difference.

That's scientifically much more interesting than saying:

“The AI seems better.”

93. The ultimate test isn't “does it make money?”

You need a hierarchy.

Level 1

Does it execute reliably?

Level 2

Does it control risk?

Level 3

Does it identify profitable signals?

Level 4

Does it outperform simple baselines?

Level 5

Does it outperform after fees/slippage?

Level 6

Does it survive different market regimes?

Level 7

Does it scale?

Level 8

Does the edge persist after deployment?

Level 9

Does it adapt faster than the market changes?

That's the actual journey.

94. One particularly important idea: separate “intelligence” from “authority”

I'd make this an explicit architectural principle.

The AI can have enormous intelligence:

analyze everything
query everything
run research
generate strategies
detect patterns
propose trades

But very limited authority:

cannot exceed risk limits
cannot withdraw capital
cannot alter security configuration
cannot disable monitoring
cannot override emergency shutdown
cannot arbitrarily modify execution rules

That gives you a system that can be extremely capable without making the model the ultimate source of truth.

95. The thing I'd explore deepest: autonomous strategy discovery

This is where your idea gets much more interesting than another “AI crypto bot.”

Imagine the system continuously doing:

Observe market

→ detect anomaly

→ form hypothesis

→ research

→ backtest

→ out-of-sample test

→ paper trade

→ evaluate

→ promote strategy

→ allocate tiny capital

→ measure

→ scale or retire

Now you're no longer just building:

an AI that trades.

You're building:

an autonomous quantitative research laboratory that can discover, test, deploy, and retire trading strategies.

That is a much deeper technical concept.

96. What I would explicitly tell the coding model NOT to do

Don't build:

one giant AI with unrestricted wallet access
an LLM directly deciding transaction parameters
a system where risk is implemented only in prompts
a bot that trades every time the model produces an answer
a backtest without realistic execution
a strategy that only works on one market regime
a “confidence” number with no calibration
an AI that automatically rewrites its own production strategy
a system with one RPC/data provider
a system with no immutable audit trail
a system where the strategy can override risk controls
a system where the same component controls strategy, risk, wallet, and execution

Those architectural decisions will make debugging and eventual public deployment dramatically harder.

97. What I would tell the coding model to optimize for

Not:

maximum number of trades

Not:

maximum raw ROI

Not:

maximum AI complexity

Instead:

robustness

risk-adjusted expectancy

execution quality

adaptability

observability

security

reproducibility

strategy diversity

capital efficiency

survivability

The architecture I'd give the coding model

At the highest level:

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │     DATA LAYER      │
                         │ Solana / Market /   │
                         │ Wallet / Social     │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │   MARKET STATE      │
                         │ Canonical normalized│
                         │ state representation│
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    │
                 ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                 │                  │                  │
                 ▼                  ▼                  ▼
          ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
          │ AI TRADER   │   │ SIGNAL BOT  │   │ SPECIALIZED  │
          │             │   │             │   │ AI TRADER    │
          └──────┬──────┘   └──────┬──────┘   └───────┬──────┘
                 │                 │                  │
                 └─────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ OPPORTUNITY ENGINE  │
                         │ rank / compare /    │
                         │ confidence / EV     │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ PORTFOLIO MANAGER   │
                         │ allocation /        │
                         │ correlation /       │
                         │ capital efficiency  │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │    RISK ENGINE      │
                         │ HARD LIMITS /       │
                         │ CIRCUIT BREAKERS    │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘
                                    ▼
                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ EXECUTION ENGINE    │
                         │ quote / route /     │
                         │ slippage / fees /   │
                         │ transaction         │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘

                              ┌────────────┐
                              │  SOLANA    │
                              └─────┬──────┘

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │   RECONCILIATION    │
                         │ actual chain state  │
                         │ vs internal state   │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ PERFORMANCE ENGINE  │
                         │ PnL / risk /        │
                         │ execution / alpha   │
                         └──────────┬──────────┘

                         ┌─────────────────────┐
                         │ RESEARCH / LEARNING │
                         │ discover / test /   │
                         │ promote / retire    │

That, to me, is the version of your idea worth pursuing.

The AI isn't the trading system. The AI is one class of decision engine inside a much larger autonomous financial machine.

And the really ambitious version isn't “GPT trades Solana.”

It's:

a system that can discover whether a trading idea has an edge, test it against history, observe it in real time, deploy it under strict risk constraints, measure whether it continues working, and autonomously reduce or retire it when the edge disappears.

That is the part I'd dive deepest into.



1. The core research problem: distinguish economic activity from blockchain activity

This is probably the single most important idea.

Your bot should stop thinking:

Volume = buying interest

Holders = distribution

Whale = smart money

Price increase = demand

Many wallets = many participants

Instead ask:

What economic process generated this observed activity?

For every signal, the model should be asking:

Who generated it?

How many independent entities are actually involved?

What capital was genuinely introduced?

How much activity is recursive/circular?

What happens when the activity stops?

2. Build a “market authenticity” layer

Before the strategy even asks whether to buy something, it should produce a separate assessment:

Market Authenticity

Something like:

genuine participation
uncertain
coordinated
manipulated
toxic
untradeable

This should be independent of bullish/bearish prediction.

A token can be:

very bullish but highly manipulated

or:

slightly bullish and extremely organic

Those are very different trades.

3. Wallet clustering should be one of the deepest areas of research

Don't count addresses.

Count probable economic entities.

Research ways to identify:

common funders
common withdrawal destinations
synchronized behavior
repeated transaction structures
timing relationships
identical trading patterns
shared infrastructure
common deployer relationships
common token launch history
recurring wallet families
wallet creation timing
common SOL funding sources
common interactions with specific programs

You want:

500 addresses

to potentially resolve into:

7 probable actor clusters.

That changes the entire interpretation of the market.

4. Build an entity graph, not a wallet list

Think of the ecosystem as a graph.

Nodes:

wallets
tokens
programs
pools
deployers
funding wallets
exchanges
bridges
launchpads
market makers

Edges:

funded
transferred
traded
created
interacted
deployed
received
sold
routed through
co-occurred

Then calculate things like:

“How tightly connected is this token's apparent holder base?”

A supposedly broad holder distribution might turn out to be one connected cluster.

5. Detect funding-chain relationships

One particularly important signal:

Wallet A buys token.

But where did A's SOL come from?

Maybe:

A ← B ← C ← deployer

Now A isn't independent.

You want to recursively analyze funding flows, subject to a sensible depth/time horizon, and determine whether apparently independent buyers have common upstream sources.

This is much more interesting than simply checking holder count.

6. Detect synchronized wallet behavior

Look for many wallets performing nearly identical actions:

same block/slot
same timing
same trade size ratios
same route
same sequence
same entry window
same exit window

The closer the synchronization, the less likely the wallets represent independent natural demand.

You don't need certainty.

You need:

probability of coordination

7. Detect “manufactured holder count”

This is directly related to what you described.

A token can have:

10,000 holders

but the actual ownership distribution may be concentrated into a relatively small number of entities.

Research:

cluster-adjusted holder count
effective holder count
entropy of ownership
concentration after wallet clustering
top-cluster ownership
cluster-adjusted Gini coefficient
holder independence score

The goal is:

10,000 addresses ≠ 10,000 participants

8. Research fake volume detection

Don't just use raw volume.

Build a decomposition of volume.

Ask:

How many unique economic entities generated it?
How much is back-and-forth?
How much occurs among related wallets?
What percentage is repetitive?
What percentage is profitable?
What percentage reverses quickly?
Is volume accompanied by net capital inflow?
Is volume accompanied by expanding independent participation?
Does volume disappear when incentives disappear?

A token with $10M volume and $50k net new capital is fundamentally different from a token with $10M volume and $7M net new capital.

9. Study “volume quality”

I would create an explicit Volume Quality Score.

Potential components:

independent participants
net capital flow
trade-size diversity
time distribution
buy/sell asymmetry
wallet diversity
route diversity
cluster concentration
recurrence
reversal rate

The strategy should care much more about:

quality-adjusted volume

than raw volume.

10. Study wash trading signatures

Research patterns such as:

repeated wallet-to-wallet cycling
repeated same-size trades
rapid buy/sell reversals
coordinated clusters trading among themselves
volume spikes with little net position change
synchronized activity
artificial liquidity support
activity concentrated around specific intervals

But don't create brittle “if X, scam” rules.

The system should learn behavioral signatures.

11. Research fake liquidity

This is different from fake volume.

You need to ask:

Can I actually exit?

Measure:

liquidity depth
liquidity concentration
LP ownership/control
liquidity changes over time
effective executable depth
price impact at various liquidation sizes
liquidity resiliency
liquidity withdrawal behavior

The important quantity isn't:

liquidity = $500k

It's:

How much can I actually sell right now without destroying myself?

12. Simulate your own exit before entering

This is a massive concept.

For every proposed position, the system should hypothetically ask:

“Suppose I needed to exit this entire position right now. What would happen?”

Then:

“What if liquidity fell 25%?”

“What if 50%?”

“What if the top liquidity provider disappeared?”

“What if five large wallets sell simultaneously?”

This makes the system think like a risk manager rather than a gambler.

13. Build an adversarial liquidity model

The market shouldn't be treated as passive.

Assume other actors may react to you.

Ask:

If this trade becomes crowded, what happens?

If the deployer knows traders are entering, what can they do?

If market makers pull liquidity, how quickly does exit quality deteriorate?

If several bots detect the same signal, does the edge survive?

That is much closer to the real game.

14. Analyze deployer history

The deployer should be treated as an entity with a history.

Research:

previous token launches
launch timing
token survival
liquidity behavior
wallet relationships
recurring counterparties
repeated metadata patterns
common funding sources
prior crashes
prior suspicious distributions

Then ask:

What is the deployer's historical behavior across previous projects?

This can be far more informative than looking at the current token alone.

15. Analyze creator/deployer networks

One deployer wallet may not tell you much.

Maybe the same actor has used:

20 deployer wallets
14 funding wallets
6 LP wallets
30 “community” wallets

The graph should try to discover that.

This becomes essentially:

adversarial entity intelligence

16. Study launch mechanics

Different launch mechanisms produce different behavioral signatures.

The system should know whether a token originated through:

launchpad
bonding curve
direct mint
liquidity pool creation
migration mechanism
custom program

Then adjust its expectations.

Don't use one universal token-risk model.

17. Research program-level behavior

This is a major Solana-specific advantage.

Don't just analyze tokens.

Analyze the programs responsible for the activity.

Questions:

What program executed the trade?
Is it known?
How does this program behave?
What instructions are being invoked?
Are there unusual CPIs?
Are there custom transfer restrictions?
Are there unusual account relationships?

The bot should understand the transaction's structure rather than treating transactions as opaque “buys.”

18. Token authority analysis needs to be extremely deep

At minimum research:

mint authority
freeze authority
upgrade authority where relevant
token program
Token-2022 extensions
transfer fees
default account state
transfer restrictions
permanent delegate-type capabilities
metadata authorities
other extension behaviors

Solana's Token Extensions can introduce functionality such as transfer fees and default account states, meaning a token should not be treated as equivalent to a plain historical SPL token merely because the ticker and decimals look normal.

19. Build a “can this token hurt us?” classifier

Separate from:

Will price go up?

The bot needs:

What mechanisms exist for this asset to behave unexpectedly?

Examples:

transfer fee
frozen accounts
unusual extensions
authority risks
malicious/custom programs
liquidity control
extreme concentration

That produces a structural risk score.

20. Research “honeypot-like” behavior

Not necessarily literal Ethereum-style honeypots.

Think broader:

Can the bot enter but fail to exit under realistic conditions?

Test:

small buy
small sell
simulated larger sell
expected output
actual execution path
transfer behavior
changing fees
liquidity availability

A token being purchasable isn't sufficient.

21. Build a “tradeability” score separate from liquidity

Liquidity:

“There is money here.”

Tradeability:

“I can enter and exit predictably.”

A token might have considerable liquidity but still have terrible:

slippage
volatility
execution reliability
concentration
route stability
22. Study time-dependent manipulation

Your scammer examples point toward an important idea:

The state of a token is a movie, not a screenshot.

The system should continuously model:

What's changing?

Not just:

What's the current number?

For example:

Liquidity:

$100k → $180k → $350k → $140k

is much more informative than:

current liquidity = $140k

23. Every signal should have a trajectory

For each important metric track:

current value
rate of change
acceleration
stability
historical percentile
cross-metric relationships

Examples:

volume accelerating
liquidity flat
holders accelerating
unique clusters flat

That combination may be suspicious.

24. Study contradictions between signals

This could be extremely powerful.

Suppose:

price ↑

volume ↑

holder count ↑

Looks bullish.

But:

unique economic entities ↓

cluster concentration ↑

net new capital flat

That tells a completely different story.

The bot should search aggressively for signal contradictions.

25. Build a causal hypothesis layer

Instead of just:

bullish signals = buy

the system should ask:

What mechanism would cause these observations?

Example:

Hypothesis A

Organic adoption.

Hypothesis B

Insider accumulation.

Hypothesis C

Wash trading.

Hypothesis D

Momentum bots chasing each other.

Hypothesis E

Market maker inventory behavior.

Then determine which hypothesis best explains the evidence.

That is much closer to actual trading intelligence.

26. This is where your specialized AI could become genuinely interesting

Give the model the ability to reason over:

observations → competing explanations → evidence → counterevidence → probabilities

For example:

“Volume is high.”

Instead of:

BUY

AI says internally:

“There are four plausible explanations.”

Then investigates them.

That is a much scarier system.

27. Give the AI permission to disprove itself

This should be built into the methodology.

For every bullish thesis:

Find evidence that would make this thesis false.

For every suspicious thesis:

Find evidence that would rescue it.

This prevents confirmation bias.

28. Build an adversarial “red team trader”

This might be one of your best ideas.

Have one AI whose explicit job is:

Destroy the proposed trade.

Strategy engine says:

BUY TOKEN X

Red-team agent asks:

How could this be manipulated?
What am I missing?
Could these wallets be coordinated?
Is volume fake?
Is liquidity fake?
Could this be an exit trap?
What happens if deployer sells?
Could this be a reflexive bot cascade?
What breaks our thesis?

Then the risk engine decides.

29. Add an “attack simulator”

This is where I'd really push the research model.

Given the current market state, simulate hypothetical adversarial events:

Scenario:

Top cluster sells 20%.

What happens?

Scenario:

LP falls 40%.

Scenario:

Three major wallets exit simultaneously.

Scenario:

Volume drops 80%.

Scenario:

Price gaps down 25%.

Scenario:

Transaction execution becomes 2× more expensive.

Scenario:

The dominant market maker disappears.

Then calculate:

Does the position survive?

30. Stress testing should be asymmetric

Don't simulate only:

normal conditions ±5%.

Crypto doesn't work that way.

Test:

10%
20%
30%
50%
80%

moves.

And importantly:

liquidity collapse + price collapse simultaneously.

31. Study reflexive bot cascades

Your scenario:

Scam token → lots of bots buy → scammer sells → bots detect selling → bots sell → crash

is an example of reflexivity.

The bot needs to recognize when:

market participants are mostly algorithms responding to each other's signals.

That is a different market from one dominated by organic humans.

Potential signals:

highly synchronized reaction times
repeated strategy footprints
predictable exit thresholds
homogeneous trade sizes
similar route selection
rapid cascading activity
32. Learn to identify “bot-on-bot” markets

A token can look highly liquid because hundreds of bots are fighting over it.

That's not necessarily healthy liquidity.

You want to estimate:

What fraction of activity is likely algorithmic?

And:

How stable is that liquidity if the shared signal disappears?

33. Build a “signal crowding” metric

Suppose 50,000 tokens exist, but suddenly 200 bots all respond to:

liquidity + volume + holder growth

They may all enter simultaneously.

That can create:

signal → synchronized buying → artificial momentum → signal strengthens → more buying

Then:

signal weakens → everyone exits

This is extremely important.

Your bot should ask:

Am I trading an underlying phenomenon, or a feedback loop between bots?

34. Study transaction ordering / MEV as part of market structure

Jito bundles execute transactions sequentially and atomically within a bundle, while bundle selection is competitive and based on blockspace/auction economics. That means bundle-aware actors can meaningfully affect execution dynamics and your assumptions about what happens around your transaction.

Your model should therefore understand:

transaction ordering
bundles
priority fees
leader timing
inclusion probability
execution competition
atomic sequences

Don't treat the chain as:

“I send transaction → transaction occurs.”

The actual process is more complicated.

35. Research “pre-trade state” versus “post-trade reality”

For each trade, save:

Before

What the bot believed.

During

What execution actually encountered.

After

What happened.

Then compare.

This lets you discover:

“Our liquidity model systematically overestimates executable depth.”

or:

“Our smart-money classifier works only for wallets older than X.”

That's how the system improves.

36. Build a failure taxonomy

Don't just record:

loss

Record:

Why did we lose?

Potential categories:

bad prediction
manipulation
fake volume
wallet misclassification
liquidity collapse
execution failure
slippage
latency
market regime shift
crowding
strategy overfit
signal decay
token structural risk
unexpected protocol behavior

Then you can answer:

What actually kills our system?

37. Study false positives more than successful trades

This is a major point.

Your most valuable dataset may be:

Things that looked exactly like winning trades but weren't.

Find cases where:

volume looked strong
holders grew
price accelerated
whales appeared
liquidity looked healthy

but the trade failed.

Those examples teach the classifier what traps look like.

38. Create a “near miss” database

Not just:

trades we took.

Also:

opportunities we rejected that subsequently exploded.

and:

opportunities we rejected that subsequently crashed.

This teaches the system:

Which warning signs were real versus false alarms?

39. Optimize for survival first

For this sort of system, I'd genuinely consider the first objective function:

Probability of surviving 1 year

rather than:

maximum return.

Because a bot that survives long enough to discover its edge has enormous optionality.

A bot that achieves +500% and then experiences one catastrophic failure isn't impressive.

40. Don't train on surviving tokens only

Huge survivorship bias.

If your dataset only contains tokens that still exist, you will badly underestimate:

rug probability
liquidity collapse
failed projects
abandoned tokens
scam behavior

Your dataset must contain the graveyard.

41. Build a “dead token corpus”

Collect examples of:

rugs
crashes
abandoned projects
liquidity pulls
manipulated launches
fake-volume projects
coordinated wallet schemes

Then ask:

What did these look like before they failed?

That's probably more valuable than another thousand successful tokens.

42. Also build a “legitimate winner corpus”

You don't want a paranoia machine that rejects everything.

Collect:

legitimate launches
organic growth
genuine viral adoption
sustainable liquidity growth
healthy holder expansion
long-duration winners

Then teach the model:

Manipulation and genuine growth can both look explosive.

Its job is to distinguish them.

43. Study early-stage information sparsity

The earlier you enter, the less evidence exists.

Therefore confidence should depend heavily on:

information completeness

A brand-new token should not be judged with the same standard as one with hours/days of history.

44. Confidence should be a function of both signal and evidence

Conceptually:

Signal strength × evidence quality × independence × execution quality

not just:

signal strength

45. Model unknown unknowns

This is difficult but extremely important.

The model should have an explicit state:

I don't understand this market well enough to participate.

That can happen when:

unusual program
novel launch mechanism
conflicting data
insufficient history
extreme volatility
unknown wallet clusters
unusual liquidity structure

“No trade” is a feature here.

46. Give the system a novelty detector

Ask:

Have we seen anything like this before?

If not:

lower confidence / research only / smaller exposure

This protects the system from novel scam mechanisms.

47. Research anomaly detection separately

You could have a dedicated subsystem looking for:

“This does not look like normal Solana market behavior.”

Signals might include:

unusual transaction graph
unusual wallet creation
abnormal synchronization
abnormal liquidity movement
abnormal buy/sell sequence
unexplained volume
unusual program interactions

That anomaly engine feeds all three trading modes.

48. Create a “token dossier”

Before the strategy evaluates a token, generate a structured dossier containing:

Identity
mint
program
decimals
metadata
Authorities
mint
freeze
relevant extension authorities
Liquidity
pools
depth
concentration
changes
Participants
holders
clusters
funding relationships
Behavioral
volume
trade distribution
buy/sell dynamics
timing
History
deployer
related tokens
related wallets
Execution
expected slippage
routing
transaction conditions
Risk
structural risk
manipulation risk
liquidity risk
execution risk
model uncertainty

Then the AI isn't staring at random APIs. It's analyzing a coherent object.

49. Keep “facts” separate from “interpretations”

This is critical for your AI.

Facts

34% of supply belongs to cluster X.

Interpretation

likely coordinated ownership.

Never merge them.

Otherwise the model starts treating its own guesses as facts.

50. Keep competing hypotheses simultaneously

The model should be able to maintain:

H1: organic demand — 45%

H2: coordinated accumulation — 30%

H3: wash trading — 20%

H4: unknown — 5%

Then update as evidence arrives.

That's much more robust than:

“Bullish.”

51. Bayesian thinking could be very useful here

You don't necessarily need an explicit textbook Bayesian model everywhere.

But conceptually:

prior belief

→ new evidence

→ likelihood of each explanation

→ updated belief

That is exactly the behavior you want.

52. Research survival-analysis approaches

Instead of:

Will token go up?

Consider:

What is the probability this token is still healthy after 5m / 15m / 1h / 6h?

That can be incredibly useful.

A token may have high expected upside but poor survival probability.

53. Research hazard models

Potentially estimate hazards like:

liquidity collapse
major insider sell
price crash
abandonment
manipulation unwind

Then the portfolio engine can ask:

Is the expected reward worth the hazard?

54. Use multiple time scales

A token could be:

5-minute bullish

but:

1-hour toxic

and:

1-day dead

Your model should reason at multiple horizons.

55. Analyze “who is making money”

This is a surprisingly powerful lens.

Don't only ask:

Who is buying?

Ask:

Who is consistently winning?

Then:

identify repeat winners
cluster them
determine their behavior
detect whether they lead or follow
evaluate whether their actions are predictive

A wallet repeatedly buying tokens before major expansion is potentially more valuable than 10,000 generic holders.

But again, you need enough history to avoid mistaking luck for skill.

56. Don't blindly follow profitable wallets

This creates copy-trading reflexivity.

The moment your bot and everyone else's bot follows the same wallets:

the signal changes.

Your system should estimate:

signal persistence

and

signal crowding.

57. Model strategy interaction

Your three modes can be used against each other.

For example:

Deterministic strategy

BUY

General AI

BUY

Specialized AI

WAIT

Red-team AI

high manipulation probability

Then the system could reduce allocation.

This is where an ensemble becomes much more valuable than a single “smart” agent.

58. Make the AI compete with simple rules

This is essential.

For each strategy, compare against:

random
buy-and-hold
momentum baseline
volatility baseline
simple liquidity filter
simple wallet-flow strategy

If GPT can't reliably beat a simple rule after costs, the expensive intelligence layer isn't justified.

59. Measure marginal intelligence

For every added component ask:

Did this actually improve risk-adjusted returns?

Example:

social AI:

+2% ROI

but

+20% drawdown.

Probably bad.

On-chain clustering:

-5% raw ROI

but

-40% catastrophic losses.

Could be extremely valuable.

This is how you avoid feature bloat.

60. The scariest bot won't necessarily trade the most

This is an important mindset shift.

A genuinely formidable bot could spend enormous amounts of time doing:

nothing

while waiting for:

high-quality information + favorable market structure + executable opportunity + low manipulation probability.

That's much scarier than a bot constantly firing trades.

61. Build “why not?” before “why?”

For every trade:

Why should we buy?

But more importantly:

Why shouldn't we buy?

Make the second question mandatory.

62. Build an “assumption ledger”

Every trade should have explicit assumptions:

liquidity remains above X
cluster X does not sell
expected execution price remains valid
strategy signal persists
market regime doesn't change
token remains tradeable

Then continuously monitor assumptions.

When an assumption breaks:

the trade thesis is automatically reconsidered.

That is a very powerful design.

63. Thesis invalidation should be dynamic

Don't just use:

stop loss = -10%.

Instead:

What event proves the original thesis wrong?

Maybe:

smart-money cluster exits
liquidity falls
organic participation disappears
volume quality collapses
market regime changes

This makes exits conceptually much more intelligent.

64. Distinguish price stop from thesis stop

A price can fall 8% and still have a valid thesis.

A token can rise 15% while the thesis becomes invalid.

The AI should understand that difference.

65. Consider second-order signals

First-order:

whale bought.

Second-order:

whale bought → copycat wallets followed → price rose → volume increased → momentum bots entered.

Third-order:

momentum bots entered → liquidity became crowded → whale sells → cascade.

Your bot should eventually reason about those chains.

That's where the system starts becoming genuinely sophisticated.

66. Think like an adversarial game theorist

Ask:

If I were the scammer, what would I do to fool this bot?

Then build defenses.

If your bot rewards:

rapid holder growth

someone will manufacture wallets.

If it rewards:

volume growth

someone manufactures volume.

If it rewards:

whale accumulation

someone creates fake whales.

If it rewards:

social mentions

someone manufactures social activity.

If it rewards:

liquidity

someone temporarily seeds liquidity.

This is the Goodhart's Law problem of autonomous trading.

67. Therefore keep changing what the model rewards

Never let one simple metric become the system's definition of quality.

Use many independent measurements.

And continuously test whether those measurements are being gamed.

68. I would literally create a “bot hunter” subsystem

This is one of the most interesting ideas I'd explore.

Its job isn't to find trades.

Its job is:

Find actors trying to exploit the trading algorithm.

It can study:

emerging manipulation patterns
repeated scam architectures
new wallet-cluster structures
new launch patterns
new fake-volume techniques
strategies exploiting predictable bot behavior

This becomes the immune system.

69. And the immune system should learn faster than the trader

Trader asks:

What's profitable?

Security/intelligence engine asks:

How are people trying to fool us?

Those should be separate objectives.

70. The ultimate system becomes an adversarial ecosystem

I would eventually envision:

Trader AI

tries to make money.

Risk AI

tries to protect capital.

Red-team AI

tries to disprove trades.

Market intelligence AI

tries to understand participants.

Research AI

tries to discover new strategies.

Adversarial AI

tries to discover ways the entire system could be exploited.

And below all of them:

deterministic execution/risk infrastructure.

That is much closer to the “scary effective” thing you're imagining.

What I'd tell the coding/research model to prioritize

Don't tell it:

“Build the best Solana trading AI.”

Give it these research objectives instead:

Tier 1 — Survival
Detect manipulated markets.
Detect coordinated wallet clusters.
Detect fake/circular volume.
Detect fake holder growth.
Detect liquidity traps.
Detect token authority/extension risks.
Detect deployer/creator relationships.
Detect abnormal program behavior.
Estimate executable liquidity.
Model catastrophic exits.
Tier 2 — Market understanding
Build wallet/entity graphs.
Build token dossiers.
Build market-state representations.
Detect bot-heavy markets.
Detect crowded signals.
Detect market regimes.
Detect contradictions between signals.
Model competing explanations.
Estimate information freshness.
Measure signal reliability.
Tier 3 — Actual alpha
Find predictive wallet behavior.
Find predictive transaction patterns.
Find predictive liquidity patterns.
Find predictive launch behavior.
Find predictive market regimes.
Find cross-signal interactions.
Discover new signals automatically.
Test whether signals survive after fees/slippage.
Test whether signals survive manipulation.
Test whether signals survive crowding.
Tier 4 — Autonomous learning
Maintain trade memory.
Maintain failure memory.
Maintain near-miss memory.
Generate hypotheses.
Backtest hypotheses.
Run walk-forward validation.
Paper trade.
Shadow trade.
Promote successful strategies.
Retire degraded strategies.
Tier 5 — Adversarial intelligence
Assume all observable metrics can be gamed.
Build synthetic manipulation scenarios.
Red-team every strategy.
Search for ways the strategy can be exploited.
Detect bot-on-bot cascades.
Detect signal crowding.
Detect coordinated actor networks.
Detect novel manipulation mechanisms.
Penalize unexplained market states.
Prefer no-trade over uncertainty.
And the biggest conceptual change I'd make

Your original question is basically:

“Can I make an AI that becomes a great trader?”

I would change it to:

“Can I build an autonomous system that understands the participants, incentives, topology, liquidity, execution mechanics, and adversarial behavior of a market well enough to know when it has a genuine exploitable edge?”

That is a much harder question.

But it leads you toward something substantially more interesting.

The genuinely dangerous version of this system isn't the AI that can look at a chart and say BUY.

It's the system that looks at:

4,800 wallets
17 suspected clusters
3 funding trees
2 liquidity providers
14,000 transactions
6 interacting programs
3 possible manipulation hypotheses
current execution depth
recent market regime
historical behavior of related deployers
behavior of known profitable wallets

and concludes:

“The apparent $2.4M volume is mostly economically dependent activity. Two clusters account for most of the acceleration. The liquidity is less resilient than reported. The recent holder expansion is largely synthetic. There is a 71% probability this is a reflexive bot-driven move. Expected upside does not compensate for the probability of liquidity collapse. Do nothing.”

And then, 90 seconds later, it sees a different token where the evidence lines up and says:

“This one is different.”

That distinction between superficially identical market states is where I would spend the majority of the research effort.

One technical constraint is worth keeping in view: Solana transaction state is very time-sensitive—recent blockhashes expire quickly, RPC nodes can disagree or lag, and confirmation itself has important failure modes—so your “intelligence” layer ultimately has to feed a tightly controlled execution/reconciliation layer rather than assume its observed state remains valid while it deliberates.

And I would absolutely make adversarial simulation a first-class component, not something added later. The bot should regularly be asked:

“Assume somebody knows exactly what our algorithm rewards. How would they manufacture the appearance of a perfect trade?”

Then make the system beat its own attack scenarios.
